composition: The specimen belongs to a low-alloy steel with nominal composition (wt.%): 0.398 C, 0.87 Mn, 0.31 Si, 0.024 S, 0.01 P, 0.05 Ni, 0.16 Cr, 0.01 W, 0.1 V, 0.03 Mo, 0.002 Ti, 0.13 Cu, balance Fe. Iron is the matrix element; carbon and manganese define the alloy designation, while Si, Cr, V, Mo, Ti and Cu are minor alloying/residual additions. This steel is used mainly for automobile hub bearings and was supplied as hot-rolled round bars.
conclusions: This sample demonstrates that a transient temperature increase (a transient decrease of Z_P) imposed at 0.4 strain induces strong dynamic softening—the flow stress collapses from a peak of ~84 MPa to ~48 MPa—and drives the DRX fraction to ~0.99 by 0.9 strain. The final austenite grain size (79.69 ± 4.78 µm experimental) is nearly identical to that of the constant 1050 °C condition (81.30 ± 4.39 µm), confirming the CA prediction that after decreasing Z_P the two DRX grain generations quickly grow to constant-condition-like sizes and the final AGS remains essentially unchanged. This behavior contrasts with the transient Z_P increase cases, where the final AGS increases with ε_I. The close agreement between experiment and the 3D CA simulation supports the inhomogeneous-dislocation-density framework as a quantitative tool for multi-stage hot-forging microstructure control.
mechanisms: The continuous temperature rise from 950 °C to 1050 °C lowers the Zener–Hollomon parameter Z_P, which simultaneously enhances dynamic recovery (reducing average dislocation density in both the matrix and DRX grains) and increases grain-boundary mobility through faster vacancy/atom migration, thereby accelerating DRX grain growth and producing the steep flow-stress drop from ~84 MPa to ~48 MPa.

Even after the total DRX fraction reaches a level comparable to the constant 1050 °C condition, the inhomogeneous dislocation-density distribution leaves some residual matrix grains with higher dislocation density than under constant conditions; this residual stored energy drives continued growth of both first- and second-stage DRX grains, allowing the DRX fraction to exceed the constant-condition value and the stress to decrease faster.

The transient temperature change generates two DRX grain populations; second-stage DRXGs accumulate dislocation more slowly (owing to their smaller size and the grain-boundary-sliding contribution), so they have lower dislocation density than the matrix and first-stage DRXGs, enabling them to refine both the matrix and the first-stage grains.

During the temperature ramp, recrystallization refines the microstructure (AGS from ~65.33 µm at 0.4 strain to 62.63 µm at 0.5 strain), but subsequent DRX grain growth at 1050 °C causes coarsening to 79.69 µm at 0.9 strain, making the final grain size nearly equal to that of the constant 1050 °C condition.

Because the transient temperature increase leaves a higher residual dislocation density, the first-stage DRXGs can grow within a very short strain interval to sizes nearly identical to the corresponding constant-condition grains and are then progressively consumed/refined by second-stage DRXGs, so the final AGS remains almost unchanged relative to the constant condition—in contrast to a transient Z_P increase, where delayed second-stage nucleation leaves larger residual first-stage grains.
microstructure: Before deformation the material exhibited a mixed-grain austenite microstructure with a 2D average grain size (AGS) of 141.66 µm (SD 54.54 µm; range 10.22–265.20 µm). At 0.4 strain, just before the temperature rise, the specimen (still at 950 °C/0.01 s⁻¹) had an AGS of about 65.33 µm and a DRX fraction of 75.7% (experimental). By 0.5 strain, at the end of the temperature ramp, the prior austenite grains (reconstructed from as-quenched martensite) were nearly fully recrystallized with an AGS of 62.63 ± 4.11 µm (experimental) versus 65.61 µm (CA simulation), and the DRX fraction reached 0.979 (experimental) / 0.995 (CA). At 0.9 strain the experimental AGS coarsened to 79.69 ± 4.78 µm (CA: 75.90 µm) with a DRX fraction of 0.99 (experimental) / 0.998 (CA). The 3D CA model further resolves two DRX grain populations at 0.9 strain: first-stage DRXGs (950 °C, 0.01 s⁻¹) with AGS 61.89 µm and volume fraction 0.13, and second-stage DRXGs (1050 °C, 0.01 s⁻¹) with AGS 77.83 µm and volume fraction 0.86. Overall, the microstructure first refined during the temperature rise and then coarsened during continued deformation.
processing: Cylindrical specimens (ϕ 6 mm × 9 mm) were cut along the rolling direction from the hot-rolled bar and polished, with 0.1 mm tantalum foil placed between the specimen ends and the indenter to reduce friction and prevent interfacial melting. The specimen was heated to 1250 °C at 10 °C/s and held for 180 s to homogenize the austenite, then cooled to 950 °C at 10 °C/s and held for 60 s to stabilize temperature. In the first deformation stage it was hot-compressed at 950 °C and 0.01 s⁻¹ to ε_I = 0.4. The temperature was then continuously increased from 950 °C to 1050 °C over the 0.4–0.5 strain interval at 10 °C/s while maintaining 0.01 s⁻¹, after which compression continued to a total true strain of 0.9. The specimen was immediately water-quenched to freeze the high-temperature microstructure.
properties: In Gleeble 1500 hot compression, the experimental flow stress for this condition reached a peak near 84 MPa around the 0.4 strain transition and then fell steeply to ≈48 MPa by about 0.5 strain as the temperature rose to 1050 °C. The DRX fraction evolved from 0.757 at 0.4 strain to 0.979 at 0.5 strain and 0.99 at 0.9 strain (experimental), closely matched by the CA predictions 0.769 / 0.995 / 0.998. Characterization comprised optical microscopy (Olympus-GX71, picric-acid etching) for prior austenite grain observation, EBSD (SU5000 SEM, 0.65–1.3 µm step size) of the as-quenched martensitic microstructure, and ARPGE-based prior austenite grain reconstruction (GOS threshold 3°, boundaries >10°) to separate recrystallized from deformed grains and measure equivalent grain diameters.
summary: This sample is a cylindrical hot-compression specimen of a low-alloy steel (Fe-0.398C-0.87Mn) deformed under a varying-temperature schedule: first compressed at 950 °C and 0.01 s⁻¹ to a true strain of 0.4, then continuously heated to 1050 °C over the 0.4–0.5 strain interval (a transient decrease of the Zener–Hollomon parameter Z_P) at the same strain rate, and finally compressed to a total true strain of 0.9 before water quenching. It serves as one of the validation cases for a new phenomenological constitutive model and an inhomogeneous-dislocation-density 3D cellular automaton describing multi-stage dynamic recrystallization (DRX) and flow-stress softening under varying deformation conditions.
unmapped: Because both DRX grain populations are recrystallized austenite grains, they cannot be readily separated by EBSD/GOS analysis alone; their individual AGS and volume fractions at 0.9 strain (first stage 61.89 µm / 0.13; second stage 77.83 µm / 0.86) are resolved through the 3D CA model.
